talks.title: Unlocking the Potential of ChatGPT in Pentesting
talks.teaser: Explores how ChatGPT can be applied to penetration testing work.

talks.title: Aye matey! Bring home the bounty. Don't just find bugs-- Find an SSRF.
talks.teaser: Shows how to move past ordinary bug hunting toward finding a server-side request forgery worth a bounty.

talks.title: Betrayed by Your Browser: How Third-Party Tracking Systems Are Following You Online and What to Do
talks.teaser: Shows how browsers get fingerprinted and tracked by third-party systems, and practical steps to limit that exposure.
talks.summary:
Security researcher Mike Landeck opens with his research into third-party trackers on websites where people look for health help, which he says turned up 187 distinct ways a browser can be followed. He explains the basics first: cookies, hidden iframes, zero-pixel image requests, and browser fingerprinting built from details such as the user agent, screen size and default font. He points out that tracking usually depends on weakening protections a healthy cookie should have, including expiry, encryption, HttpOnly, and same-site scope.

He then walks through a case study of a family-planning website, where one page load produced hundreds of requests to dozens of domains, many of them tracking services. Some of the outside content came from a component with a known exploitable flaw, so a trusted site inherits the risk of every third-party script it loads. He compares browsers and notes that Brave's fingerprint protection can break sites that use fingerprints for session handling, which is why he personally favours Firefox with privacy extensions and a VPN, while accepting that these are only partial layers.

For AppSec and privacy teams, the closing advice is to treat tracking code as part of design, privacy impact assessments and testing, to check tags against the EFF's published tracker list, to use Content Security Policy to restrict what scripts can do, and to re-review third-party code after release. He also shows simple configuration changes, such as anonymizing IP addresses in Google Analytics.

talks.title: Catch Me If You Can: Hunting Cloud Exfiltration Using Anomaly Detection
talks.teaser: Shows how anomaly detection and conventional queries can surface cloud data exfiltration hidden among normal API activity.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with public cloud exfiltration cases from 2016 to 2021, several of which went unnoticed until a later retrospective response. The speaker argues that defenders struggle to separate attacker API activity from legitimate automation, because stolen credentials produce calls that look like ordinary work. Many of these intrusions need no endpoint foothold at all, only valid keys or tokens.

Using AWS CloudTrail as the main data source, the talk explains which events matter for exfiltration, such as bucket listing, snapshot sharing and database snapshot restores, and why enriching events with geography and network name helps. It demonstrates hunts built on new or rare combinations of user, service, action and network, along with error spikes and volume outliers, run in a notebook. One case examined an S3 request using temporary credentials from an unexpected network, which traced back to a web application design rather than an intruder.

The closing section covers early-warning signals, such as list-bucket calls that tend to precede bulk transfers, and the trade-offs of automatically interrupting access. The main takeaway is to combine conventional alerting with anomaly detection, keep noisy signals in hunting workflows rather than paging queues, and agree on response processes with the teams that depend on automation.

talks.title: Command, Control, and memes: Cordyceps + ant = zombie
talks.teaser: Shows how a red team deploys, configures and secures C2 infrastructure, and automates it with infrastructure as code.

talks.title: Never Break the Chain: Attack Chaining for 0-Days
talks.teaser: Shows how small, separate flaws combine into critical exploit chains, from file upload abuse to SQL injection and command injection.
talks.summary:
Erica frames the talk around automating exploit chains, where several small weaknesses, some newly found, combine into one serious compromise. She argues that a low-severity finding becomes critical once paired with another flaw, and that a clear business impact, such as server takeover, is easier to get accepted.

Her cases come from real engagements and bug bounty work, with details redacted. An admin panel accepting Java archive uploads let her run code, and the process reported system-level rights, a reminder that environment data can mislead testers. Cross-site scripting fed a Windows batch script for command injection. A report generator that trusted client-side content led to a shell, and an unsupported comment plugin with a hardcoded key let her spoof users. A path traversal flag overwrote site content, and unsalted, reused password hashes paired with SQL injection granted admin access. Error-based injection got past keyword filters, with help from a language model suggesting alternative syntax.

The defensive takeaways are to restrict uploads and control egress, prefer allowlists, avoid hardcoded keys and home-grown crypto, salt hashes, retire unsupported software, and layer filtering. She closes by discussing bug bounty negotiation and vulnerability disclosure programs.

talks.title: Cyber Espionage and the Global Power Struggle: A Deep Dive
talks.teaser: Explains how states and commercial vendors use iPhone zero-days to pursue geopolitical goals, and what that means for defenders.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a common frustration: news of a new iPhone zero-day often arrives as a CVE number and a severity score, with no indicators that defenders can hunt for. The speaker, a cyber threat intelligence analyst, uses that gap to ask who actually buys and deploys these exploits. Reported cases involving NSO Group spyware cover journalists, the fiancée of a slain reporter, a royal family's ex-spouse and associates, and officials in several countries, with a recurring focus on human rights and state-on-state targeting.

The middle section turns to data. It draws on a Google Threat Analysis Group report on commercial surveillance vendors, which tied a large share of 2023's actively exploited zero-days to such vendors, and on CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list for iPhone flaws from the same year. Cross-referencing those sources, the speaker found that roughly half of the iPhone entries were linked to highly targeted use against journalists or democratic opposition. The argument is that attribution matters both for governments deciding on deterrence and for private defenders judging how much a given zero-day actually threatens their organisation. The talk then widens into geopolitics, covering Gulf states' cyber investment, sport and events as soft power, a Saudi-funded golf league, new semiconductor plants in Arizona, and Chinese actors targeting edge devices that lack endpoint detection.

The closing takeaways are practical. Scale concern to the targeting profile rather than to headlines, inventory and log edge devices, and weigh vendor and partner choices against the competitive and geopolitical context of the business. Most real-world compromises still come from older, already patched vulnerabilities, and the speaker notes that data on economic espionage and insider threats remains thin.

talks.title: Exploring RMM Tools and Their Forensics
talks.teaser: Shows how remote management tools leave forensic traces and which artifacts help investigators confirm their use.
talks.summary:
Responders often struggle to find accurate, current guidance on remote monitoring and management tools, remote access software and remote desktop applications. The speaker describes outdated comparison articles, vendor-only documentation, and a case where an unfamiliar remote tool was installed by an attacker. Legitimate tools also blur the line between approved use and abuse, which makes attribution harder.

The approach was to set up clean Windows 11 virtual machines, install each application, and record the files it wrote before and after first use, along with its network behavior. Because these tools must beacon out to relay servers, network monitoring can reveal their presence even when endpoint inventory is incomplete. For AnyDesk, a connection trace file on the target host shows that a session was actually established, and it can expose the connecting IP, a session identifier, a linked account email, and recent file-transfer folders.

The talk stresses that Windows event logs rarely capture the install or ongoing use of these tools, so artifacts often sit in application data folders or the registry. In one case, blocking a tool's published domains on a Friday likely prevented a weekend ransomware deployment. Practical takeaways include standardising on a small approved set of remote tools, blocking unapproved ones by their documented domains and ports, and checking older guidance against current versions.

talks.title: DON’T PANIC!: An IR Guide to Communicating with Execs
talks.teaser: Shows how to write incident updates for executives that drop jargon, stick to facts and focus on business impact.
talks.summary:
Three security leaders from the financial sector open by framing the problem: incident responders must explain technical events to executives and other non-specialists who need to make business, risk, regulatory or insurance decisions. They note that the same approach suits any emergency communication, from fire departments to schools.

The core guidance is to lead with business impact, such as customer, financial and reputational effects, and keep reports short, ideally a few paragraphs. Writers should stick to known facts, use qualifiers when something is uncertain, avoid speculation and emotional language, and answer likely questions before they are asked. A useful structure starts with a bottom-line-up-front summary, then the response actions underway, with lessons learned added in later updates and a formal root cause report kept separately. Three before-and-after rewrites cover a ransomware intrusion, a zero-day in a widely used product, and a misconfigured device tied to a former employee's lingering access. The revised versions replace acronyms and framework references with plain descriptions and concrete counts, and they remove alarmist claims while noting the actions being taken.

The closing advice covers timing and review. Send an early update even when information is thin, tell executives when the next one will arrive, and account for regulatory or contractual deadlines. Some teams assign a separate person to handle communications so responders can keep working. Finally, have someone outside security with editing skills review drafts, and treat feedback as a way to improve.

talks.title: From Cyber Lemons to Lemonade: A Refreshing Take on Exposed Data
talks.teaser: Shows how breach dumps and infostealer logs can be searched and used to answer investigative and defensive questions.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a former federal agent who now teaches SANS courses, argues that exposed data is already part of attackers' routines. Citing a government analysis of breaches, he notes that valid credentials were the starting point in more than half of them. He covers the legal and ethical questions around breach data, including recent Justice Department guidance that emphasizes intent and passive collection, and explains where he personally draws the line on buying stolen data.

He describes the main categories: raw breach dumps, combo lists of deduplicated credentials, marketing datasets, and infostealer logs taken from infected machines. He reviews where this material is sold or shared, from paid lookup services with limited search to criminal marketplaces selling remote access. For very large files, he recommends command-line tools and building an index with a fast search utility, and he advises caution because stolen data often carries malware.

Real cases show practical uses: matching leaked password hashes to explain a wave of account takeovers, tracing a help desk social engineering attempt to a public breach, and finding a contractor credential and a VPN key in infostealer output so affected organizations could be warned early. He closes by pointing to monitoring, archived web pages, and torrent catalogs as sources, with the takeaway that defenders benefit most by learning about exposure before attackers act.

talks.title: SBOMs for Evil: Turning Un-Remediated Software Supply Chain Documentation into an Attack Path
talks.teaser: Shows how software bills of materials, enriched with CVE and threat data, can expose attack paths in embedded devices.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with what a software bill of materials (SBOM) is: an inventory of the components, versions and dependencies inside a firmware image or application. The speaker explains how SBOMs are produced through source code analysis or binary analysis, compares the CycloneDX and SPDX formats, and shows how CPE matching links listed components to known CVEs. He also covers the regulatory pressure pushing vendors to supply SBOMs, including FDA submission requirements, US federal procurement rules and the EU Cyber Resilience Act.

The middle of the talk is a case study on OpenWrt, an open source Linux firmware widely used as the base of consumer IoT products. A binary analysis of an OpenWrt image produced more than 1,500 findings, with 10 critical and 38 high. One flagged component, the LuCI web interface, carried a 2019 CVE. Commercial threat intelligence feeds had no exploit data for it, so the speaker found a public proof of concept through community contacts and reviewed it. Shodan results suggested tens of thousands of internet-facing hosts with the same interface. OpenWrt's git-based version strings also failed to match the CPEs in the NVD. A live demo against an old OpenWrt virtual machine showed command execution and file creation, while the final shell step was not completed on stage.

The closing argument is that the same enriched inventory helps defenders decide which devices to patch, how to segment networks and what to monitor. VEX statements can document components whose vulnerable code is never reached. The speaker also warns that shared SBOMs tend to spread publicly, so organizations should assume adversaries can use them.

talks.title: Simple Ways to Make Webhook Security Better
talks.teaser: Surveys how webhook providers verify senders and shows practical checks consumers can add to incoming events.
talks.summary:
Scott McAllister introduces webhooks as HTTP callbacks in which a provider pushes event notifications to an endpoint the consumer supplies. A plain listener has no built-in way to know whether a request truly came from the provider, whether its contents were changed, or whether it was replayed. He demonstrates this with a small note app receiving real Twilio text messages, then sends a hand-crafted POST that the app accepts just as readily.

The core of the talk surveys verification patterns gathered from more than a hundred providers. He covers one-time endpoint verification at subscription time, shared secrets, HMAC signatures over the request body, asymmetric key signing, mutual TLS, data-less notifications that require a follow-up API call, and timestamp-based replay prevention. For each he weighs setup effort, what it protects and where it falls short, such as missing confidentiality or the burden of key rotation. HMAC is the most common choice in the research.

He closes with advice for both sides: providers should document verification thoroughly and show it end to end, and consumers should use whatever checks a provider offers. In the demo, adding token-based verification causes unsigned requests to return 403 Forbidden, both in a local development setup and in a production setup using an SDK-driven tunnel.
